summary: At an annual Senate hearing, Sen. Bob Menendez, who is charged with bribery, asked four big-bank CEOs how much their firms had returned to consumers at the CFPB's direction, and none could answer. He cited figures totaling nearly $4 billion to argue that financial regulation helps customers, and he defended the CFPB against a Supreme Court funding challenge. He also pressed the CEOs on overdraft fees, praising Citigroup for eliminating them and urging the others to follow.
one_line: Indicted Sen. Bob Menendez quizzed four bank CEOs on CFPB-ordered consumer payouts, none could answer, and he pressed them on overdraft fees and CFPB funding.
key_facts: Sen. Bob Menendez (D-N.J.) questioned four retail bank CEOs at a Wednesday Senate hearing about how much their firms returned to customers at the CFPB's direction, and none could answer.
The CEOs questioned were Jamie Dimon (JPMorgan Chase), Brian Moynihan (Bank of America), Jane Fraser (Citigroup) and Charles Scharff (Wells Fargo).
CFPB-ordered payouts cited: $360 million for JPMorgan Chase, $819 million for Bank of America, $1 billion for Citigroup and over $2 billion for Wells Fargo, nearly $4 billion in total.
Menendez said over $4 billion was returned to consumers in the past dozen years.
In September, the Justice Department charged Menendez and his wife Nadine with accepting bribes and allegedly using his Senate seat to improperly aid the Egyptian government; he pleaded not guilty.
A raid of Menendez's house turned up $100,000 in gold bars and bundles of cash stuffed into jacket pockets.

The CFPB was created in 2011 after the 2008 Financial Crisis and faces a Supreme Court case brought by the Community Financial Services Association of America, which argues it is unconstitutional because it is not subject to annual congressional appropriations.
Menendez warned the lawsuit could upend every rule, guidance and order the CFPB has issued, which he called dangerous to the financial system.

The hearing featured eight executives and covered new rules requiring big banks to hold larger capital reserves; the banks said the rules would limit lending to lower and middle income buyers, while chair Sherrod Brown said banks prefer riskier, higher-return investments.
A 2021 study found Hispanic Americans paid $3.1 billion a year in overdraft fees and Black Americans $1.4 billion.
Citigroup eliminated overdraft fees in 2022; Fraser told Menendez the bank is still profitable and the change did not upend its business model.
JPMorgan Chase eliminated overdraft fees under $50 in 2021, and overdraft revenue still rose 3% in 2022, per Bloomberg.
Wells Fargo gave customers a 24-hour grace period on overdrafts, and Bank of America cut its overdraft fee from $35 to $10.
